title: Coulomb's law (magnitude of electrostatic force)
body: |\vec F_E|=\frac{1}{4\pi\epsilon_0}\frac{|q_1q_2|}{r^2}=k\frac{|q_1q_2|}{r^2}
ced_evidence: 8.1.A.2 "directly proportional to the magnitude of each of the charges and inversely proportional to the square of the distance"

title: Direction of the electrostatic force
body: The force is along the line of separation between the objects: like signs repel, opposite signs attract.
ced_evidence: 8.1.A.3 "along the line of separation between the objects"; 8.1.A.3.i, 8.1.A.3.ii

title: Elementary charge and charges of particles
body: The elementary charge e is the magnitude of the charge of one electron or proton, the smallest indivisible amount of charge; an electron has charge −e, a proton +e, and a neutron has none.
ced_evidence: 8.1.A.1.ii–iii "the elementary charge e"

title: Charge as a scalar
body: Charge is a scalar quantity described as positive or negative.
ced_evidence: 8.1.A.1.i "Charge is a scalar quantity"

title: Point charge
body: A point charge is a model in which the physical size of a charged object or system is negligible in the context of the situation being analyzed.
ced_evidence: 8.1.A.1.iv "A point charge is a model"

title: Electric vs. gravitational force
body: Electrostatic forces can be attractive or repulsive while gravitational forces are always attractive; between two charged masses the gravitational force is usually much smaller, but gravity dominates at large scales because large systems tend to be electrically neutral.
ced_evidence: 8.1.B.1–8.1.B.3 "gravitational forces are always attractive"

title: Limit on discrete-charge force calculations
body: Calculations of electric force are expected for four or fewer interacting charged objects, or more only in situations of high symmetry.
ced_evidence: Boundary Statement 8.1 "four or fewer interacting charged objects or systems"

title: Electric permittivity
body: Electric permittivity measures the degree to which a material or medium is polarized in the presence of an electric field, and free space has a constant value ε₀.
ced_evidence: 8.1.C.1 "degree to which a material or medium is polarized"; 8.1.C.3 "Free space has a constant value of electric permittivity"

title: Electric polarization
body: Polarization is the induced rearrangement of electrons by an external electric field, separating positive and negative charge within a material or medium.
ced_evidence: 8.1.C.2 "induced rearrangement of electrons by an external electric field"

title: Conductor vs. insulator
body: Conductors are made of electrically conducting materials in which charge carriers move easily; insulators are made of nonconducting materials in which charge carriers cannot move easily.
ced_evidence: 8.1.C.4.ii "charge carriers move easily"

title: Conservation of charge
body: Any change in a system's net charge is due to a transfer of charge (typically electrons) between the system and its surroundings; otherwise the net charge stays constant.
ced_evidence: 8.2.A.2 "Any change to a system's net charge is due to a transfer of charge"; 8.2.A.2.ii

title: Induced charge separation
body: Induced charge separation occurs when the electrostatic force between two systems alters the distribution of charges within them, polarizing one or both, and it can occur in neutral systems.
ced_evidence: 8.2.A.1.ii–iii "Induced charge separation"

title: Grounding
body: Grounding is electrically connecting a charged object to a much larger, approximately neutral system such as Earth.
ced_evidence: 8.2.A.3 "Grounding involves electrically connecting a charged object to a much larger and approximately neutral system"

title: Definition of electric field
body: \vec E=\frac{\vec F_E}{q}
ced_evidence: 8.3.A.2 "ratio of the electric force exerted on a test charge at the point to the charge of the test charge"

title: Test charge
body: A test charge is a point charge small enough in magnitude that its presence does not significantly affect the electric field in its vicinity.
ced_evidence: 8.3.A.2.i "A test charge is a point charge of small enough magnitude"

title: Direction of the electric field and force
body: The field points away from isolated positive charges and toward isolated negative charges, and the force on a positive test charge is in the direction of the field.
ced_evidence: 8.3.A.2.ii–iii "points away from isolated positive charges and toward isolated negative charges"

title: Superposition of electric fields
body: The net electric field at a location is the vector sum of the individual fields created by nearby charged objects.
ced_evidence: 8.3.A.3.i "vector sum of individual electric fields"

title: Electric field map and field line diagram
body: Field maps use vectors to show field magnitude and direction at many locations; field line diagrams are simplified models giving relative magnitude and direction at any position.

items.label: Field map vectors
items.meaning: arrow direction and length show direction and magnitude at many locations

items.label: Field lines
items.meaning: line direction shows field direction, and the relative magnitude can be read from the diagram

ced_evidence: 8.3.A.3.ii–iii "Electric field maps use vectors"

title: Conductor in electrostatic equilibrium
body: Excess charge lies on the surface, the field inside the conductor is zero, and the field at the surface is perpendicular to it.
ced_evidence: 8.3.B.1 "electric field within the conductor is zero"; 8.3.B.1.i

title: Insulator in electrostatic equilibrium
body: Excess charge is distributed throughout the interior as well as the surface, and the field inside may be nonzero.
ced_evidence: 8.3.B.2 "distributed throughout the interior of the insulator"

title: Field outside a spherically symmetric charge
body: Outside an isolated sphere with spherically symmetric charge, the field equals that of a point charge of the same net charge at the sphere's center.
ced_evidence: 8.3.B.1.ii "same as the electric field due to a point charge"

title: Electric field of a charge distribution by integration
body: \vec E=\frac{1}{4\pi\epsilon_0}\int\frac{dq}{r^2}\,\hat r
ced_evidence: 8.4.A.1 "found using integration and the principle of superposition"

title: Distributions requiring calculus for E
body: The charge distributions and locations for which calculus-based field derivations are expected.

items.meaning: Infinitely long, uniformly charged wire or cylinder, at a distance from its central axis
Thin ring of charge, at a location along the axis of the ring
Semicircular arc or part of one, at its center
Finite wire or line charge, at a point collinear with the line charge
Finite wire or line charge, at a location along its perpendicular bisector

ced_evidence: Boundary Statement 8.4 "only expects students to use calculus to find the electric field"

title: Use symmetry to simplify field analysis
body: Symmetry of a charge distribution can simplify finding the electric field it produces.
ced_evidence: 8.4.A.2 "Symmetry considerations of certain charge distributions"

title: Electric flux, uniform field
body: \Phi_E=\vec E\cdot\vec A
ced_evidence: 8.5.A.2 "electric field E that is constant across an area A"

title: Electric flux, general surface integral
body: \Phi_E=\int\vec E\cdot d\vec A
ced_evidence: 8.5.A.3 "surface integral of the electric field over the surface"

title: Area vector direction and sign of flux
body: The area vector is perpendicular to the surface's plane and points outward from a closed surface, and the sign of the flux comes from the dot product of E and A.
ced_evidence: 8.5.A.2.i–ii "perpendicular to the plane of the surface and outward from a closed surface"

title: Flux
body: Flux describes the amount of a given quantity that passes through a given area.
ced_evidence: 8.5.A.1 "amount of a given quantity that passes through a given area"

title: Gauss's law
body: \oint\vec E\cdot d\vec A=\frac{q_{\text{enc}}}{\epsilon_0}
ced_evidence: 8.6.A.1 "relates electric flux through a Gaussian surface to the charge enclosed by that surface"

title: Gaussian surface
body: A Gaussian surface is a three-dimensional, closed surface, and the total flux through it does not depend on its size if the enclosed charge is constant.
ced_evidence: 8.6.A.2–8.6.A.3 "three-dimensional, closed surface"

title: Choosing a Gaussian surface
body: Construct the surface so the enclosed charge's field is perpendicular or parallel to each region of the surface, simplifying the surface integral, and apply it quantitatively only for spherical, cylindrical, or planar symmetry.
ced_evidence: 8.6.A.4 "either perpendicular or parallel to different regions of the Gaussian surface"; Boundary Statement 8.6

title: Area and enclosed charge for a cylindrical Gaussian surface
body: For cylindrical symmetry the flux goes through the curved lateral area 2πrl (not πr² or 4πr²), and the enclosed charge uses the charged shell's actual radius with the correct density type (σ for surface, ρ for volume).
caution: State the lateral area 2πrl and use the shell's radius R, not the Gaussian radius r, when writing q_enc from a surface density.
ced_evidence: 8.6.A.4 "simplified surface integral"; 8.6.A.5 charge from density

title: Total charge from a charge density
body: Q=\int\lambda\,d\ell\;(\text{1D}),\qquad Q=\int\sigma\,dA\;(\text{2D}),\qquad Q=\int\rho\,dV\;(\text{3D})
ced_evidence: 8.6.A.5 "integrating the charge density over the length (one dimension), area (two dimensions), or volume (three dimensions)"

title: Maxwell's equations
body: Maxwell's equations are the collection of equations that fully describe electromagnetism, and Gauss's law is Maxwell's first equation.
ced_evidence: 8.6.A.6 "Gauss's law is Maxwell's first equation"
